pi.name: Dunpeng Cai
pi.title: Assistant Professor
bio: Dunpeng Cai studies the cellular and molecular processes that contribute to vascular and heart valve disease. His research brings together mechanistic studies and experimental disease models to investigate aneurysm, aortic valve calcification, vascular remodeling, and inherited vascular disorders.

Dr. Cai completed his doctoral and postdoctoral training at the University of Missouri. His work combines molecular approaches, imaging, and microsurgery to connect discoveries in cells and tissues with questions relevant to cardiovascular treatment.

research.title: Aortic valve disease
research.summary: Understanding how cellular signaling and inflammation contribute to the stiffening and calcification of the aortic valve.
research.body: We connect observations in human valve tissue with experimental studies to examine disease mechanisms. Current work investigates DOCK2 signaling and uses translational models to explore potential therapeutic targets for aortic valve calcification.

research.title: Vascular remodeling & aneurysm
research.summary: Investigating how vascular cells and the extracellular matrix change during aneurysm and vascular disease.
research.body: Our studies examine smooth muscle cell plasticity, endothelial inflammation, and matrix remodeling. By identifying molecular pathways that shape these responses, we seek to understand how vascular structure and function are lost and how they might be preserved.

research.title: RNA approaches to genetic disease
research.summary: Exploring RNA-based approaches to the molecular causes of inherited vascular disease.
research.body: Our Marfan syndrome research investigates strategies to correct disease-associated fibrillin-1 transcripts. This work asks whether RNA editing can provide a route toward addressing the genetic basis of vascular disease, with efficacy and translation remaining research goals.

research.title: Models that connect mechanism to disease
research.summary: Developing experimental platforms to study cardiovascular disease and investigate potential interventions.
research.body: Our published work includes humanized aortic valve calcification models, models of flow-driven pulmonary hypertension, and vascular repair studies. These platforms help connect molecular questions with tissue remodeling and cardiovascular function.
